newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China readies next HK milestone -- new legislature.
newsitem.headline: China readies next HK milestone -- new legislature.

text.p: Having made history by choosing Hong Kong's post-colonial leader, China is now preparing another milestone -- setting up a highly controversial provisional legislature for when the British pull out next year.
The move is likely to cripple the present Legislative Council, elected in 1995, because more than half its members -- the speaker included -- have bid for seats on the provisional body.
China, upset by electoral reform in the twilight of British rule, has sworn to install an interim assembly to replace Hong Kong's elected council after the handover next July 1.

The Beijing-controlled Selection Committee will meet in the Chinese city of Shenzhen on Hong Kong's border next Saturday to pick the legislature's 60 members from a list of 130 -- all of whom have already been closely vetted by China.
Last week the committee made history by selecting Hong Kong's first Chinese leader, former shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa, who will take the helm in Hong Kong on July 1.

The colonial government has vowed never to cooperate with the provisional legislature, regarding it as unconstitutional to have two legislatures operating at the same time -- even if one is only enacting laws for after the handover.

The issue threatens to rock the boat and prolong handover quarrels between the incoming sovereign and departing Governor Chris Patten's administration up to the final minute of British rule in 198 days.
The pro-democracy movement in Hong Kong has condemned the move by China as a way to snuff out democracy in the territory.
The Democratic Party, the territory's largest, has boycotted the contest for seats on the interim body, despite pleas by Chief Executive-designate Tung to join.
Tung has urged the Democrats, vocal critics of Beijing, to stop confronting China and run for seats on the interim body.
The current list of candidates makes it a left-wing monopoly. Of the 130, 91 are also members of the Selection Committee, which is deciding the composition of the assembly.
As things stand, the controversial assembly will be dominated by pro-Beijing parties.

Tsang Yok-sing, leader of the biggest pro-China political party, the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment of Hong Kong, last week said there was room for compromise among those seeking seats. This sparked fears the parties would make an under-the-table deal, leaving little room for independent candidates.

"Public confidence will sink to rock bottom if, as the independents fear, there is no room in the debating chamber for the colour and vibrancy which comes from a disparate collection of opinion," the South China Morning Post commented on Friday.
Even Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen called on the political parties last Thursday to refrain from horse trading.
"We have to stop some factions or groups from making under-the-table deals," Qian said.

"The composition of the provisional legislature must be broadly representative, must show a balanced participation of every sector of the community, and its members must be selected upon upon their representativeness in the community, their personalities and their constitutional experences," Qian said.
